title: A Friendly Robot Still Needs to Earn Your Trust
summary: Park's EMBRACE invited talk explored how companion robots can encourage connection without letting affection obscure privacy risks.

sources.label: Read Chorong Park's original LinkedIn post

paragraphs.text: A robot can feel caring without giving someone enough control. Chorong Park explored that tension as the first invited speaker at the EMBRACE workshop during IEEE RO-MAN 2026 in Kitakyushu, Japan, on August 24.

Drawing on community engagement and a study with 22 older adults, Park discussed how pet-like movement, expressive faces, and responsive timing can invite affection. Familiar interactions and reminiscence were also part of the research she described.
But warmth can complicate trust. Park raised the possibility that emotionally appealing behavior may make people less alert to privacy risks, even when an interaction feels comfortable.

Her response was to design for understandable behavior, meaningful control, and consent people can withdraw. The goal is not to remove emotion from companion robots, but to keep a friendly interaction from becoming a reason to overlook boundaries.

The workshop connected that question with perspectives on emotion, culture, aging, and care. Park left with new questions about how robots might support connection while respecting the person making it.
